title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
Heirs’ property can arise when real estate passes to family members after an owner dies without a clear transfer of title. When an estate is never formally settled, ownership can splinter across descendants while the deed remains unchanged.1 Family members may legally inherit an interest in the property, a shared arrangement known as tenancy in common, without holding the clear title needed to manage it.
Without a clear title, families may struggle to sell or refinance the home, borrow against it for repairs, obtain disaster-recovery assistance, or pass it cleanly to the next generation.2 In Virginia, even someone holding a small fractional interest may seek to divide or force the sale of the property, placing the entire home at risk of purchase by real estate investors.3
Left unresolved, heirs’ property can stunt generational wealth, especially for African American and working class families, as property becomes difficult to keep, cutting families off from many of the basic benefits of homeownership and opening pathways to involuntary land loss.






In an effort to better understand the landscape of heirs’ properties in Virginia, this study examines parcels showing signs of tangled or unresolved title concentrated across six jurisdictions in the Richmond–Petersburg region.
The study region covered Richmond City, Henrico, Colonial Heights, Chesterfield, Hopewell, and Petersburg.





With over 380,000 parcels across the six study areas, identifying heirs’ property can be a challenge.
Heirs’ property is difficult to identify from public records alone. A deed may remain in the name of someone who has died, while the people who inherited the property never appear in county assessor’s data.





Instead of combing through each parcel individually, this study developed a weighted screening index to identify parcels showing combinations of indicators commonly associated with heirs’ property.4
Each parcel was screened using a combination of ownership, owner-name, tenure, vacancy, mailing-address, and deceased-owner indicators.
Click an indicator for a short definition.

  
    Ownership
    County records list several people, or an estate, as owners of the
    same parcel. Ownership split across many people is a common result of a
    property passing to multiple heirs without a settled estate.
  
  
    Owner name
    The name recorded on the deed carries heirs language, such as
    “estate,” “heirs,” “et al,” or “life estate,” rather than a single
    living owner. This wording often appears when a property has passed to
    survivors without the title being formally transferred into their
    names.
  
  
    Tenure
    The deed has not changed hands for decades. A very long gap since the
    last recorded transfer can mean the original owner has died and the
    records were never updated.
  
  
    Vacancy
    The U.S. Postal Service marks an address as vacant when mail has gone
    undelivered there for an extended period. A home that sits vacant while
    its deed stays unchanged is a common sign of an unsettled estate.
  
  
    Mailing address
    The owner’s tax bill is mailed to an address different from the
    property itself. After an owner dies, bills often go to a relative who
    lives elsewhere while the property stays in the deceased owner’s name.
  
  
    Deceased owner
    Public records indicate that the person named on the deed has died.
    This is the strongest single indicator, because it means the property may
    never have been formally passed on to the heirs.
  

Those signals were then weighted and combined to distinguish parcels with stronger evidence of unresolved title from those with less conclusive patterns.
Parcels were placed into four tiers based on the strength of that evidence.

High confidence parcels show stronger, converging evidence of unresolved title.
Likely parcels show meaningful but less conclusive evidence.
A smaller group of parcels showed some signals, but not enough together to sort clearly into either tier above.
The majority of parcels fall into this tier. These properties show few or none of the ownership signals above, so there is no meaningful evidence of an unresolved estate.


These tiers are classifications built from the indicators above, not definitive determinations of heirs’ status.

The result is a regional screen identifying parcels with an elevated risk of being an heirs’ property. More details of the screening methodology are available on the Methods & Data page.

3. Map of Heirs’ Properties
Across Richmond, Petersburg, Hopewell, Colonial Heights, Chesterfield, and Henrico, the study screened 381,852 parcels for signs of an heirs’ property.

  
    381,852

    of the regional parcel stock. That’s around one in every 47 parcels
  

The screen identified 8,091 parcels with elevated heirs’ property risk, combining the high confidence and likely heirs tiers. That is equal to 2.12% of the regional parcel stock, or about one in every 47 parcels.
Of those properties, 1,225 were classified as high confidence, meaning several strong indicators pointed toward an unresolved estate. Another 6,866 were classified as likely, meaning the available records showed meaningful but slightly less conclusive evidence.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
4. Key Findings
The most common flagged property is an ordinary home that appears to have remained in the same family for many years without updated assessor information.
More than four out of five flagged parcels, 81.7%, have an owner of record who has died. Nearly as many, 75.8%, have been held under the same ownership for a very long time. More than two-thirds of all flagged parcels carry both signals.
Most also have only one or two owners listed in the assessor record. This means the region’s most common heirs’ property pattern is relatively simple on paper. A deceased person remains named as an owner, the deed has not changed for decades, and the property may still be occupied by family members whose ownership interests were never formally recorded.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
5. Flagged Homes vs. Regional Stock
Flagged properties also differ from the region’s housing stock as a whole.
The median flagged home was built in 1965, compared with 1981 across the full study area. Its median assessed value was $245,700, compared with $329,000 region-wide.
Vacancy is much more common among flagged parcels as well. Among properties with a known Postal Service vacancy status, 9.55% of flagged parcels were marked vacant, compared with 1.03% of all parcels.5
That difference is substantial, but it is important not to confuse heirs’ property with vacancy. Most flagged properties are not vacant. The dominant pattern remains an older, occupied home whose ownership records appear not to have kept pace with changes in the family.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
section: 6. Heirs’ Rates Change Sharply Across the Region
text:
6. Heirs’ Rates Change Sharply Across the Region
The regional average hides large differences between localities.
Petersburg has the highest flagged-parcel rate, at 4.88%.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
7. Patterns Cluster by Neighborhood
Heirs’ property risk is not randomly scattered across the region. High-rate neighborhoods tend to sit near other high-rate neighborhoods, while low-rate neighborhoods tend to sit near other low-rate neighborhoods.
The map divides the region into census tracts. A census tract is a small statistical area commonly used to describe neighborhood conditions. Tract boundaries do not always match the boundaries residents use when naming their neighborhoods, but they allow the same measures to be compared consistently across the region.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
8. Clustering Across Tracts
Heirs’ properties are not scattered randomly across the region. They tend to appear near one another, often forming neighborhood- and block-level concentrations that continue across census tract boundaries.
We measured this pattern using a spatial test called Ripley’s K. This test counts how many flagged parcels are located near other flagged parcels, then compares that result with 999 random arrangements of the same number of parcels across the region’s actual parcel stock. If location did not matter, the observed pattern and random pattern would look much the same.6
Instead, at 250 meters, flagged parcels had 61% more nearby flagged parcels than the random patterns predicted. The difference remained statistically significant at every distance tested, from 250 meters to 5 kilometers.
This means heirs’ property is not only more common in some cities or census tracts than others, it is also concentrated within neighborhoods, and those concentrations do not stop at administrative lines.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
9. Hot and Cold Spots
The neighborhoods at the two ends of the pattern differ sharply.
Residents of the 16 core hot-spot tracts are, on average, 66.1% non-Hispanic Black, compared with 8.2% in the 26 core cold-spot tracts.
The average poverty rate is 25.5% in hot spots and 3.9% in cold spots. Median household income is approximately $49,510 in hot spots, compared with $147,415 in cold spots. Housing is also substantially older, and owner-occupancy is lower.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
10. Poverty Plays a Role
Poverty is strongly associated with heirs’ property. Neighborhoods with higher poverty, lower incomes, and lower owner-occupancy generally have higher flagged-parcel rates.7
But poverty does not account for the full racial patterns in this region.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
section: 11. Today’s Heirs’ Properties Follow Historical Exclusion
text:
11. Today’s Heirs’ Properties Follow Historical Exclusion
Heirs’ properties do not appear in a vacuum.
In the 1930s, the federal Home Owners’ Loan Corporation, or HOLC, evaluated neighborhoods for mortgage-lending risk. Richmond neighborhoods received grades from A, considered the safest places for lenders, through D, labeled “hazardous.”
Black residents and other marginalized groups were routinely treated as lending risks. Neighborhoods where they lived were often assigned the lowest grade and outlined in red, or redlined. These maps helped institutionalize unequal access to mortgages, home improvement credit, and the wealth-building benefits of homeownership. The legacy of these practices is reflected in the landscape of heirs’ properties today.9

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
section: 12. There Is No Single Type of Heirs’ Property
text:
12. There Is No Single Type of Heirs’ Property
Although the study finds a clear pattern in the geography of heirs’ properties, flagged parcels do not all present the same legal or housing problem.
Using only facts recorded about each parcel, not neighborhood race, income, or poverty, the study identified four recurring property types.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
13. Different Places Require Different Approaches
The study grouped the region’s census tracts into 11 contiguous zones using SKATER, a regionalization method.12 SKATER treats the region as a network in which every tract is linked to the tracts it physically touches. It then cuts the links that join the least similar neighbors, and the groups left standing become the zones.
Because a tract can only ever be grouped with tracts it touches, each zone forms a single continuous area that can be drawn on a map, rather than a scattered collection of look-alike tracts. Each zone therefore contains neighboring tracts that are relatively similar in both their heirs’ property rates and their mixtures of the four property types.
These are analytic zones, not new neighborhoods, political districts, or service boundaries. They simplify a complex regional pattern so that outreach can respond to local conditions.

    The index begins with the facts recorded about the parcel itself: estate language in the owner name, decades without a recorded transfer, postal vacancy, a tax bill mailed somewhere other than the property, and multiple owners of record.
    A corporation cannot be an heir. Business, institutional, and government-owned records were filtered out, and the owner fields on the remaining parcels were parsed into individual person-owner records.
    Each of those person-owner records was checked against a database of deceased persons. A confirmed death on the owner of record is the strongest single signal.
    Other records add context. Long tenure, absentee ownership, multiple owners, and vacancy can strengthen the evidence of unresolved title.

    A flag is a research finding. Confirming heirs’ property status requires a legal review of deeds, probate records, and family relationships.

title: Heirs’ Property in the Richmond Region
text:
15. About This Study
This study was commissioned by the Richmond Heirs Property Network (RHPN), with funding from the Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC), to give the region its first parcel-level picture of heirs’ property. RHPN connects families with free legal assistance for resolving tangled titles, including drafting wills, probating estates, and clearing ownership records. The findings here are intended to direct that outreach, and to inform policy, toward the neighborhoods where unresolved title is most concentrated.

Tracts with fewer than 5 heirs-flagged parcels or fewer than 100 total parcels are not assigned a rate class.

title: Methods & Data
text: Heirs’ property is what happens when a property owner dies and the title never formally passes to the next owner through a clear, documented transition. The deed stays in the deceased person’s name while descendants keep living in, paying taxes on, or otherwise using the home. What the heirs hold instead is a tenancy in common: each one owns an undivided fractional interest in the whole property rather than title to a specific part of it. That gap can leave a family with clouded title and no clean authority to sell, refinance, repair, or access disaster aid, and it opens the door to partition actions by speculators.

title: Methods & Data
section: Where the Method Sits in the Research
text:
Where the Method Sits in the Research
Published heirs’ property studies generally identify likely cases in one of two ways. Some rely on ownership language in assessor records, flagging terms such as estate, heirs, or et al.1 Others compare the owner of record with death records and consider how long the deed has remained unchanged.2 This study combines both approaches and adds information on ownership structure, mailing address, tenure, and postal vacancy. Because no single indicator is conclusive, parcels are classified only when several signals point in the same direction.
The regional scope creates an additional methodological challenge. The Philadelphia tangled-title study conducted by The Pew Charitable Trusts drew from a single municipal assessment system.3 This study covers six jurisdictions, each with its own assessor data, field definitions, parcel-number formats, and recordkeeping practices. The screening process therefore required both a common regional framework and locality-specific steps for cleaning and matching records. Those decisions are documented below.

title: Methods & Data
section: The Parcel Universe and the Denominator
text:
The Parcel Universe and the Denominator
The denominator for every rate in this study is 381,852 parcels, every parcel on the assessment rolls of the six jurisdictions, spanning 258 census tracts. Parcel records come from ReGrid (Q1 2026), which consolidates county assessment rolls into a single national schema.
The six rolls otherwise share little. Land-use codes follow six different county-specific schemes that were never harmonized, use descriptions exist in only three of the six counties, and zoning frequently diverges from what actually sits on a parcel at the rural edges of the region. The study therefore uses the full parcel stock as its denominator rather than attempting a residential-only universe, for three reasons.

One fixed denominator applies the same rule in all six jurisdictions. A residential filter would have to be built six different ways from six incompatible coding schemes, putting a different error into each jurisdiction’s rate.
Heirs’ property is not confined to one land-use class. Flagged parcels include occupied family homes and inherited empty lots, and a use-class filter would have dropped real cases.
The choice is conservative. Non-residential stock in the denominator can only pull the reported rate down, consistent with reading every total in this study as a floor.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Finding Deceased Owners
The strongest single signal is a deceased owner of record. Owner fields across the six rolls were parsed into 445,287 individual person-owner records, and each was checked against a commercial deceased-suppression database built around the Social Security Administration’s Death Master File, the same industry mechanism used in tangled-title research elsewhere. The check flagged 8,676 owners of record as deceased. Where one owner holds several parcels, a confirmed death applies to each parcel that names that owner.
Death-registry matching inherits the registry’s limits. The Death Master File is known to be incomplete, so some deceased owners are missed, and that error pushes the study’s totals down, not up.

title: Methods & Data
text:
How Parcels Were Screened
Reading deeds to identify heirs’ property at scale across six jurisdictions is infeasible. Instead, the study scored every parcel on a set of ownership signals that, taken together, make heirs’ status likely. The index was built in stages.
First, the study began with the facts recorded about the parcel itself including estate language in the owner name; decades without a recorded transfer; postal vacancy; a tax bill mailed somewhere other than the property; and multiple owners of record.
Before any further data was acquired, that preliminary index was checked against actual deeds. A sample of addresses spanning high- and low-risk tiers was checked against the Virginia circuit courts’ Secure Remote Access (SRA) land-records system in order to check the logic if a low-risk parcel had come back as heirs’ property, or a deed name had failed to match the assessor’s owner of record, it would have signaled that the index was missing signals. Instead, assessor and deed names agreed on the sampled low- and moderate-tier parcels, while the high-risk parcel in the sample showed the deed/assessor mismatch the index predicted.
Second, corporations cannot be an heir’s property. Businesses, institution, and government-owned records were filtered out, and the remaining owner fields across the six assessor datasets were further parsed into around 450,000 individual person-owner records.
Third, each person-owner record was checked against a commercial deceased-suppression database built around the Social Security Administration’s Death Master File. Where one owner holds several parcels, a confirmed death applies to each parcel that names that owner. The deceased-owner match was then folded into the index alongside the parcel-facts signals, with the promotion rules described below.
Heirs’ Index Signal Set:

a deceased owner of record
explicit estate language in the owner name itself, words like HEIRS, ESTATE, LIFE ESTATE, and DECEASED6
long ownership tenure, meaning no recorded sale in twenty years or more, or no sale date on record
absentee ownership, a tax bill mailed somewhere other than the property, including out of state
multiple owners of record, meaning three or more named owners on one parcel7
USPS vacancy status8

Signals are weighted rather than simply counted, and the same weights, cutoffs, and promotion rules apply identically in all six jurisdictions.9

The composite score sorts each parcel into a tier. A score of five or more reaches High Confidence. A score of three or four accompanied by a confirmed deceased owner reaches the Likely tier. Two promotion rules then sit on top of the point total:

A parcel held by three to eight named owners where one is confirmed deceased is promoted to the High Confidence tier, as regionally this is a frequent pattern of heirs’ properties.
A parcel held by three to eight named owners whose tax bill goes to an address away from the property, an arrangement in which one sibling handles the tax bill from a different address while another lives in the home, is promoted to the Likely tier. It is weighty evidence, but it is never sufficient for High Confidence on its own.

Promotion rules can only raise a parcel’s tier, never lower one, and a deceased match alone, with no corroborating signal, does not reach either flagged tier.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Separating Businesses from Families
Asessor parcel data carries a ready-made corporate indicator, however the study tested it before trusting it alone to filter corporate properties. It failed in both directions. It missed real corporations, including some of the region’s largest institutional landholders, and it wrongly flagged people whose names merely sound like businesses, families with names like Bank, Temple, or Church, among them genuine estates.
Corporate identification was therefore done from the owner names themselves. Name rules built around business and institutional language gathered every candidate parcel into a single review list, 559 parcels in all, and every candidate was ruled on individually. Estates and family trusts were deliberately kept in the heirs population.
As mentioned, no name-based screen is perfect in either direction. A person whose surname reads as a business word can be wrongly caught, and the individual review exists to correct exactly that error. A business whose legal name reads like a person’s name can slip through, and that residual error is bounded by scale. Confirmed corporate owners amounted to well under one percent of the flagged population.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Signals Considered and Rejected
The screen’s exclusions are as deliberate as its inclusions.

Trust ownership does not fire the estate-language signal. Living trusts, revocable trusts, and family trusts are overwhelmingly estate-planning vehicles held by living homeowners, not heirs’ property. A frequency check across all six rolls found explicit testamentary trust language on only 22 of the 381,852 parcels, too few to justify a separate signal, and owner strings that also carry words like ESTATE or DECEASED fire the estate-language signal anyway.
A shared-surname signal, three or more owners sharing a last name, was designed and then dropped. Surname changes at marriage make it unreliable for women, and the multiple-owner signal already captures most of what it would have added.
A tax-delinquency signal was planned and proved impossible. The tax-amount field is empty in all six county files.
The estate keyword fires only outside the phrase REAL ESTATE, which otherwise floods the signal with property-management companies.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Data Conventions
Two conventions run through every published number, and two smaller ones are noted in the footnotes.10

Multi-lot assessments are counted once. Some properties span several recorded lots, and the assessor repeats one combined assessed value on every lot’s row. Summed naively, a single assessment would be counted once per lot; one 21-lot property in the study area would be counted twenty-one times over. Value summaries collapse each such group to a single assessment before any median or total is computed.
Census tracts are re-derived from coordinates. Each parcel’s census tract was recomputed by locating the parcel’s coordinates within tract boundaries. Raather than trust assessor data for correctly sort parcels by census geography, the study re-derived each parcel’s tract and block group based on its coordinates, constrained to the parcel’s own jurisdiction. The constraint mattered particularly at county lines, where a mapped point that drifted across a boundary would otherwise pull in a neighboring county’s tract.

title: Methods & Data
text:
How the Numbers Were Checked

The full chain from the raw death-check return to the final study population was reconciled in both directions over the entire parcel stock, not a sample, with forward traces of sampled decedents and backward traces by county and property type.
Every analysis script re-asserts the study’s locked totals before it runs, and randomized methods are seeded, so any re-run must reproduce the published artifacts exactly or fail loudly.
Key figures are also deliberately computed the wrong way, with the wrong denominator or the wrong base population, and the build fails unless the shipped number differs from the wrong one. A check that can only agree is not a check.
Every public file, including this website as rendered, passes a mechanical disclosure scan that blocks parcel-level fields, owner information, exact tract rates, and superseded figures from earlier working drafts.

title: Methods & Data
text:
What the Screen Cannot Say

It is a screen, not a title determination. No sample of flagged parcels has been taken through a courthouse title search, so the share of flagged parcels that would survive one is unmeasured. Deed-record checks are in-person work in each of six jurisdictions and sat outside this study’s scope. Public materials are worded accordingly.
The total is a floor. The screen requires convergent evidence, the death registry is incomplete, and Virginia assessors often update tax rolls to living family members while the deed stays in a deceased owner’s name, so an unknown share of true heirs’ property is invisible to owner-record screening.
Tract-level findings are ecological. The inequity results are measured on tract aggregates, the right frame for a regional study, and cannot speak to any individual owner’s race or income.
One source carries the engine signal. Most of the flagged population carries the deceased-owner signal, which rests on a single commercial death registry whose own error rate is not published.

Published materials show tract rates as ranges (bins), not exact values. Tracts with fewer than 5 heirs-flagged parcels or fewer than 100 total parcels are not assigned a rate class. 12 of 258 tracts in the study area are suppressed under that rule. title: Methods & Data
text:
Defining Heirs’ Property
Heirs’ property is what happens when a property owner dies and the title never formally passes to the next owner through a clear, documented transition. The deed stays in the deceased person’s name while descendants keep living in, paying taxes on, or otherwise using the home. What the heirs hold instead is a tenancy in common: each one owns an undivided fractional interest in the whole property rather than title to a specific part of it. That gap can leave a family with clouded title and no clean authority to sell, refinance, repair, or access disaster aid, and it opens the door to partition actions by speculators.

title: Methods & Data
section: Where the Method Sits in the Research
text:
Where the Method Sits in the Research
Published heirs’ property research relies on two main detection methods. National estimates from the Housing Assistance Council and Fannie Mae (2023) rest on owner-name patterns, words like ESTATE, HEIRS, and ET AL sitting in assessor records. New York City tangled-title research matches owner names against death records alongside deed age. This study combines both families of evidence, with postal and tenure signals added, into a single convergent screen. Implementations vary from study to study, so the choices specific to this one are documented on this page.
One structural difference shapes everything below. The best-known tangled-title work, Pew Charitable Trusts’ Philadelphia study, drew on a single city assessment office. This study spans six independent assessment operations with no shared schema, no shared parcel-numbering convention, and different data-quality habits, and several of the decisions described here exist to manage that.

Relationship to the Thomson and Bailey index
The closest published analogue is the parcel-screening index Ryan Thomson and Conner Bailey built to estimate heirs’ property extent across the South and Appalachia.13 That index scores each parcel on a small set of property-tax variables and treats a parcel as heirs’ property when the score crosses a fixed threshold. This study adapts that summative approach and departs from it in four ways.

Death is measured, not inferred. Thomson and Bailey read heirs’ status primarily from how ownership is written in the tax record. This study checks whether the named owner has actually died, which sits closer to the mechanism that produces heirs’ property in the first place.
The corroborating signals are administrative rather than building-related. Their index uses an effective-year-built variable as a proxy for the permitted improvements an heirs’ property is less likely to receive. This study instead looks for evidence that ownership and occupancy have come apart, through vacancy, multiple owners of record, and a mailing address away from the property.
Classification is tiered rather than pass/fail. A parcel in their index either crosses the threshold or does not. This study separates stronger convergent cases from lighter but still meaningful ones, which is more useful for deciding where outreach should go first.
The purpose is different. Their index had to behave consistently across millions of rural and urban parcels in eleven states. This one is calibrated to the quirks of six local assessors and to the practical question of which households may benefit from legal assistance.

In short, this study adapts the summative parcel-screening approach used in earlier heirs’ property research, and adds direct deceased-owner matching, vacancy and ownership-structure indicators, and separate confidence tiers calibrated to the Richmond region.

title: Methods & Data
section: The Parcel Universe and the Denominator
text:
The Parcel Universe and the Denominator
The denominator for every rate in this study is 381,852 parcels, every parcel on the assessment rolls of the six jurisdictions, spanning 258 census tracts. Parcel records come from ReGrid (Q1 2026), which consolidates county assessment rolls into a single national schema.
The six rolls otherwise share little. Land-use codes follow six different county-specific schemes that were never harmonized, use descriptions exist in only three of the six counties, and zoning frequently diverges from what actually sits on a parcel at the rural edges of the region. The study therefore uses the full parcel stock as its denominator rather than attempting a residential-only universe, for three reasons.

One fixed denominator applies the same rule in all six jurisdictions. A residential filter would have to be built six different ways from six incompatible coding schemes, putting a different error into each jurisdiction’s rate.
Heirs’ property is not confined to one land-use class. Flagged parcels include occupied family homes and inherited empty lots, and a use-class filter would have dropped real cases.
The choice is conservative. Non-residential stock in the denominator can only pull the reported rate down, consistent with reading every total in this study as a floor.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Finding Deceased Owners
The strongest single signal is a deceased owner of record. Owner fields across the six rolls were parsed into 445,287 individual person-owner records, and each was checked against a commercial deceased-suppression database built around the Social Security Administration’s Death Master File, the same industry mechanism used in tangled-title research elsewhere. The check flagged 8,676 owners of record as deceased. Where one owner holds several parcels, a confirmed death applies to each parcel that names that owner.
Death-registry matching inherits the registry’s limits. The Death Master File is known to be incomplete, so some deceased owners are missed, and that error pushes the study’s totals down, not up.

title: Methods & Data
text:
How Parcels Were Screened
Reading deeds to identify heirs’ property at scale across six jurisdictions is infeasible. Instead, the study scored every parcel on a set of ownership signals that, taken together, make heirs’ status likely.

a deceased owner of record, confirmed as described above
long ownership tenure, meaning no recorded sale in twenty years or more, or no sale date on record
absentee ownership, a tax bill mailed somewhere other than the property, including out of state
multiple owners of record, meaning three or more named owners on one parcel
USPS vacancy status
explicit estate language in the owner name itself, words like HEIRS, ESTATE, LIFE ESTATE, and DECEASED

Two conventions keep the multiple-owner signal honest. Parcels with nine or more owners of record are excluded from it, because at that scale the record is almost certainly a condominium or association master parcel, and parcels in the upper owner-count range were spot-checked against assessor records to confirm they are genuine family ownership situations. Where the number of owners could not be resolved from the record at all, the signal was treated as absent rather than guessed, a default that can only miss cases, never invent them.
Signals are weighted, and the strongest combinations matter more than any point total. A parcel held by multiple owners where one is confirmed deceased is the strongest pattern short of explicit estate language in the record, and it sorts to high confidence directly. Multiple owners combined with an absentee mailing address is the next strongest, the familiar arrangement in which one sibling handles the tax bill from a different address while another lives in the home, and it sorts to likely. A deceased flag alone, with no corroborating signal, is never sufficient for the high-confidence tier.
Scoring left 8,156 parcels in the two flagged tiers. Business-owned parcels were then removed, as described in the next section, to produce the final study population. High confidence parcels show strong, convergent evidence of an unresolved estate (1,225 parcels, 0.32% of the stock). Likely parcels show real but lighter evidence (6,866 parcels, 1.80%). Together they make up the 8,091-parcel study population, 2.12% of the 381,852 parcels scored.
A flag is an indicator-based screen of public records, not a legal determination of title. Because the screen requires convergent evidence, totals are best read as a floor, not a ceiling.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Separating Businesses from Families
A corporation cannot be an heir, so business-owned, institutional, and government-owned parcels had to leave the flagged population before it was final. The parcel data carries a ready-made corporate indicator, and the study tested it before trusting it. It failed in both directions. It missed real corporations, including some of the region’s largest institutional landholders, and it wrongly flagged people whose names merely sound like businesses, among them genuine estates, exactly the families this study exists to find.
Corporate identification was therefore done from the owner names themselves. Name rules built around business and institutional language gathered every candidate parcel into a single review list, 559 parcels in all, and every candidate was ruled on individually rather than in bulk. The review removed 65 parcels as corporate or institutional. Estates (373 parcels) and family trusts (121 parcels) were deliberately kept in the heirs population.
No name-based screen is perfect in either direction. A person whose surname reads as a business word, Bank or Temple or Church, can be wrongly caught, and the individual review exists to correct exactly that error. A business whose legal name reads like a person’s name can slip through, and that residual error is bounded by scale. Confirmed corporate owners amounted to well under one percent of the flagged population, so a handful of missed businesses cannot move the study’s totals.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Signals Considered and Rejected
The screen’s exclusions are as deliberate as its inclusions.

Trust ownership does not fire the estate-language signal. Living trusts, revocable trusts, and family trusts are overwhelmingly estate-planning vehicles held by living homeowners, not heirs’ property. A frequency check across all six rolls found explicit testamentary trust language on only 22 of the 381,852 parcels, too few to justify a separate signal, and owner strings that also carry words like ESTATE or DECEASED fire the estate-language signal anyway.
A shared-surname signal, three or more owners sharing a last name, was designed and then dropped. Surname changes at marriage make it unreliable for women, and the multiple-owner signal already captures most of what it would have added.
A tax-delinquency signal was planned and proved impossible. The tax-amount field is empty in all six county files.
The estate keyword fires only outside the phrase REAL ESTATE, which otherwise floods the signal with property-management companies.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Data Conventions
Four conventions run through every published number.

Vacancy rates use only parcels with a known yes or no USPS vacancy determination, roughly nine in ten parcels. Parcels with no determination are excluded from the denominator.
Some multi-lot properties repeat one combined assessment across every lot row. Value summaries collapse those groups so a single assessment is never counted more than once.
Census tract assignment was re-derived from parcel coordinates, constrained to the parcel’s own jurisdiction, rather than taken on faith from the source file.
A small number of parcels, 627 of 381,852, carry no parcel identifier in the assessor data. They remain in the denominator, and the two flagged parcels among them are identified by street address.

title: Methods & Data
section: Building on the Thomson and Bailey Index
text:
Building on the Thomson and Bailey Index
Combining the methodologies noted above, this work builds on the parcel-screening index developed by Ryan Thomson and Conner Bailey to estimate heirs’ property across the South and Appalachia.4 In short, this study adapts their summative parcel-screening approach, and adds direct deceased-owner matching, vacancy and ownership-structure indicators, and separate confidence tiers calibrated to the Richmond region.5

title: Methods & Data
text:
Parcel Universe
The denominator for every rate in this study is 381,852 parcels, every parcel on the assessment rolls of the six jurisdictions in the Richmond–Petersburg region, spanning 258 census tracts. Parcel records come from ReGrid (accessed Quarter 1, 2026), which consolidates county assessment rolls into a single national schema.
Each assessor dataset contained some shared and some diverging properties. Land-use codes follow six different county-specific schemes that are non-harmonized, and use descriptions exist in only three of the six counties. The study therefore uses the full parcel stock as its denominator rather than attempting a residential-only universe, for two reasons.

One fixed denominator applies the same rule in all six jurisdictions. A residential filter would have to be built six different ways from six incompatible coding schemes, putting a different error into each jurisdiction’s rate.
Heirs’ property is not confined to one land-use class. While a business cannot be an heirs’ property, in this region flagged parcels include occupied family homes as well as inherited empty lots, and a use-class filter across six jurisdictions raises the risk of dropping legitimate heirs’ properties.

title: Methods & Data
section: What the Index Cannot Tell Us
text:
What the Index Cannot Tell Us

It is an index, not a title determination. The design-stage deed spot check described above supported the index’s logic, but no statistically representative sample of the final flagged population has been taken through a full title search, so the share of flagged parcels that would survive one is unmeasured.
The study total is best taken as a lower limit, not an upper limit. The index requires convergent evidence, the death registry is incomplete, and Virginia assessors often update tax rolls to living family members while the deed stays in a deceased owner’s name, so an unknown share of true heirs’ property is invisible to owner-record screening.
Tract-level findings are regional-context dependent. The inequity results are measured on tract aggregates, and cannot speak to any individual owner’s race or income.
The death-suppression signals, which carries most of the flagged parcels, rests on a single commercial death registry whose own error rate is not published.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Limitations

The index is only as good as the assessor data beneath it. ReGrid consolidates each county’s assessment roll as the county last refreshed it, and those refresh dates range from 2023 to 2026 across the six jurisdictions. A property sold, probated, or re-assessed after its county’s refresh date appears in this study in its earlier state.

Assessor data can be inconsistent. Some fields are missing in every county file, and a signal that cannot be read is treated as absent. Incomplete inputs therefore suppress signals and push the totals down. Earlier heirs’ property research working from tax-assessment data reported the same behavior. Accordinly, estimates from these methods run conservative.11

title: Methods & Data
text:
What’s Not Published
Published materials show tract rates as ranges (bins), not exact values. Tracts with fewer than 100 total parcels are suppressed. No parcel-level data, owner information, or addresses appear in any public material.

title: Methods & Data
text:
Research
Published heirs’ property studies generally identify likely cases in one of two ways. Some rely on ownership language in assessor records, flagging terms such as estate, heirs, or et al.1 Others compare the owner of record with death records and consider how long the deed has remained unchanged.2 This study combines both approaches and adds information on ownership structure, mailing address, tenure, and postal vacancy. Because no single indicator is conclusive, parcels are classified only when several signals point in the same direction.
The regional scope creates an additional methodological challenge. The Philadelphia tangled-title study conducted by The Pew Charitable Trusts drew from a single municipal assessment system.3 This study covers six jurisdictions, each with its own assessor data, field definitions, parcel-number formats, and recordkeeping practices. The screening process therefore required both a common regional framework and locality-specific steps for cleaning and matching records. Those decisions are documented below.
